claims.text: Progressive creep deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed primarily by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation and transfer rather than bulk activation processes.
Compositional gradients and lattice distortions at nanoscale interfaces cause interface-mediated processes to dominate the creep response.
The initial coatings have a nanoscale FCC/BCC multilayer architecture.
The initial coatings have homogeneous interface chemistry.
The initial coatings have uniform layer thickness.
Interface chemistry will be varied systematically by introducing composition gradients.
Multilayer thickness will be varied systematically.
The relevant test regime consists of sustained loading at elevated temperature and applied stress sufficient to produce creep.
The chemical and structural characteristics of nanoscale interfaces mediate dislocation nucleation.
The chemical and structural characteristics of nanoscale interfaces mediate dislocation mobility.
Tailored interfacial regions promote localized dislocation nucleation.
Tailored interfacial regions promote dislocation transfer between FCC and BCC layers.
Enhanced interfacial activity lowers the activation barrier for dislocation motion.
Lowering the activation barrier for dislocation motion produces a higher creep rate.
Engineering interface chemistry and changing layer thickness will measurably change creep rate relative to the homogeneous baseline.
Engineering interface chemistry and changing layer thickness will shift the dominant deformation mode relative to the homogeneous baseline.
The baseline multilayers exhibit progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading.
The proposed mechanism is limited to regimes in which the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact and sustained loading produces creep deformation.
